entities.name: Deutsche Oper Berlin
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Deutsche Oper Berlin, founded in 1912 in the Charlottenburg district of what was then a separate city from Berlin, is Germany's largest opera house by seating capacity (1,865 seats) and — alongside the Berlin State Opera and Komische Oper — forms Berlin's unique three-opera-house system that has no parallel in any other world city. The original building, designed by Heinrich Seeling in neo-classical style, was destroyed in Allied bombing (1943); the current brutalist building by Fritz Bornemann was opened in 1961.

The Deutsche Oper's 1912 founding reflected the democratic aspirations of Charlottenburg's bourgeoisie: unlike the royal Berlin State Opera (founded by Frederick the Great), the Deutsche Oper was built by the citizens of Charlottenburg as a 'people's opera house' — without royal patronage and with seats priced for middle-class audiences. It premiered as the 'Deutsches Opernhaus Charlottenburg' and quickly established itself as a rival to the court opera.

The Deutsche Oper today is particularly renowned for its Richard Strauss and Verdi tradition, its commitment to grand opera stagings (its stage is among Europe's largest), and its world-premiere recording of works including Richard Strauss's Arabella with the Berlin Philharmonic. It is also the site of one of opera's most notorious incidents: in 2006, General Intendant Kirsten Harms canceled a controversial production of Mozart's Idomeneo (which included a scene depicting the severed heads of Mohammed, Jesus, Buddha, and Neptune) due to terrorism fears — a decision that sparked an international debate about self-censorship in the arts.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Deutsche Oper Berlin — Germany's largest opera house, the democratic citizens' alternative to royal court opera, part of Berlin's unique three-house system, and the site of the 2006 Idomeneo self-censorship scandal — has been at the center of German operatic culture and arts freedom debates for over a century.
